description: Deep Time Division built Kasa: a globe simulation that reads any place on Earth like a core sample. It fuses NASA POWER climate records with GIBS satellite imagery to track a decade of change, then applies Mann-Kendall and Theil-Sen trend testing to separate statistically significant shifts from natural variability. Every claim is backed by a p-value, not a guess. Team locked. Live demo ready.
summary:
Kasa is an interactive Earth-observation tool that helps people investigate long-term environmental change at any place on Earth. Users spin a 3D globe, select a location, scrub through comparable NASA satellite imagery, and inspect climate trends from NASA POWER data.

For each location, Kasa removes seasonal effects from monthly temperature and rainfall data, then applies a Mann-Kendall trend test and Theil-Sen slope to distinguish meaningful trends from random variation. It presents the result in plain language without claiming causation. Users can also compare two years with a swipe view, explore place history, see OpenStreetMap roads and buildings, and ask grounded questions about the available evidence.

The project addresses the “Be an Earth System Trend Detective” challenge by making scientific environmental analysis understandable, visual, and accessible to non-specialists. It can help students, communities, researchers, and decision-makers explore how places are changing over time.
details:
Kasa turns a geographic location into an explorable environmental “core sample.” The interface begins with a 3D Earth and lets users select any point or search for a place. The camera transitions into a detailed map where users can inspect NASA satellite imagery across multiple years.

The imagery uses NASA GIBS MODIS Terra surface-reflectance composites. Each selected year uses the same calendar date so that comparisons are more consistent. Users can also compare two years side by side with a draggable swipe divider.

Kasa retrieves monthly temperature and precipitation data from NASA POWER. It removes the seasonal cycle, aggregates the results by year, and calculates a Mann-Kendall trend test with a Theil-Sen slope. The application displays annual anomalies, slope, p-value, and a carefully worded verdict. It explains that a statistical trend is not proof of causation.

Additional features include place search and reverse geocoding, Wikipedia and Wikidata context, OpenStreetMap roads and building footprints, street labels, and a grounded AI assistant. The assistant only uses information already loaded for the selected location and shows its supporting context.

The project was built with React, TypeScript, MapLibre GL JS, Vite, NASA GIBS, NASA POWER, OpenStreetMap-based services, Wikipedia, Wikidata, and an OpenAI-compatible language-model API. Kasa is creative because it combines satellite time travel, statistical testing, map exploration, and transparent scientific caveats in one approachable interface.
